findings.claim: A computational metric can enter a human HR meeting as a preassembled accusation, narrowing the practical purpose of review even when the formal meeting is labeled an effort to understand.
limits: One litigated factual record; no universal Amazon policy finding.

findings.claim: Warehouse quota law demonstrates that the metric, quota, personal work-speed denominator, adverse action and safety boundary can be made separately addressable.

Platform-work law demonstrates a stronger model: human decisions for termination-equivalent detriment, intelligible reasons, competent review, rectification, health-risk assessment and responsibility despite external vendors.

Speed and deactivation systems create the same burden question as Chloe’s meeting: who owns the metric, context, support, interim restriction, human judgment and later reconciliation when the worker experiences one coherent threat?
limits: Chloe remains a non-AI baseline and no causal equivalence is asserted.

observations.claim: In Moses v. Amazon, the reported record states that a computer system generated 205 minutes of time off task and that a manager and HR business partner held a seek-to-understand meeting.
limits: One case; system type and full policy not recovered.

observations.claim: California AB 701 requires covered employers to provide quota descriptions and allows workers to request the most recent 90 days of personal work-speed data in specified circumstances.
AB 701 protects meal, rest and safety rights and creates a rebuttable retaliation presumption for certain adverse actions following quota-data requests or complaints.
OSHA has issued enforcement releases concerning ergonomic hazards and inadequate medical care at Amazon fulfillment centers.
limits: Historic sites and cited conditions; not every facility or current practice.

observations.claim: The EU Platform Work Directive requires a human being to take decisions to restrict, suspend or terminate a contractual relationship or account or impose equivalent detriment.

The Directive provides reasons, explanation, competent contact, review, rectification, recurring impact evaluation and psychosocial-risk controls, and applies duties even when an external service provider manages the system.

title: Metric discipline, work-speed control, and deactivation
